title: Narconomics: How to Run a Drug Cartel
author: Tom Wainwright
note: Mandatory Karpathy review. Investigative economic explanation, not operational criminal instruction or routine marketing advice. Production, supply chains and market constraints are central; policy is an application, so T12=0. Cross-national scope gives T11=0. Reform advocacy alone does not establish V6. Interviews and observable incentives support the argument, but corporate analogies are not causal identification. No serious veto established. Named expert praise from Moises Naim and Misha Glenny is reproduced by the publisher; reader response is strongly positive.
notes: Reporting and interviews support observed practices; hidden-market estimates and analogical inference need caution.
Connects cultivation, distribution, competition, enforcement and international substitution.
Useful lessons about bottleneck targeting, price transmission and responses to regulation.
Explains monopsony and displacement mechanisms, though causal estimates remain limited.

Good logistics and institutional fit; limited engineering or industrial precision.

title: Leading Matters: Lessons from My Journey
author: John L. Hennessy
note: Mandatory Karpathy review, not selected for broad reader acclaim. Retained under H7's exception for organizing skilled technical work, and the scientific/technology memoir exception under V3. Institutional leadership rather than personal optimism is central; V7 is not established. Stanford and US institutional experience predominate, T11=-10. T12=0: technical organization and education, not political power. Lessons cross the author's career rather than reconstructing one historical period. Self-selection and broad virtues lower evidence and mechanism scores; no serious veto established.
notes: First-hand experience is relevant but selected success stories provide limited tests of the lessons.
Connects university leadership, entrepreneurship and philanthropy, with limited technical or economic depth.
Some reusable judgments about institutional mission and collaboration; much advice is familiar.
Cases illustrate choices without isolating their causal contribution to success.
D=5.5, moderate confidence from contents, AACSB review and reader reports. Institutional examples add context, but general virtues and repeated success references reduce learning yield.
Basic organizational principles endure despite named contemporary examples.
Relevant to research organization, less to technology mechanisms.
Distinguished computer scientist and university leader with direct experience; endorsements often come from associates.
Accessible thematic chapters, but readers report generalized or dry storytelling.
Plain expression, with some broad leadership language.

title: Super Thinking: The Big Book of Mental Models
author: Gabriel Weinberg; Lauren McCann
note: Mandatory Karpathy review. Inspected publisher sample and introduction characterize a cross-domain explanatory synthesis of reasoning models, not a specialist technical curriculum. Some productivity advice is present, but personal life support is not established as the dominant purpose; V7 is not inferred from the self-help genre label. Reasoning models and organizational applications are central, not a philosophy treatise; T12=0. No serious foundational failure established. Broad claims about the models' coverage exceed what the examples prove and reduce E.
notes: Established concepts are summarized, but analogy across domains and sweeping coverage claims have weaker support.
Links statistics, constraints, incentives and decisions; integration sometimes amounts to juxtaposition.
Useful prompts for checking a decision, with lower novelty for an experienced quantitative reader.
Explains familiar mechanisms but provides limited tests of when a transferred model fails.
